# Functions that resolve the DECLARED module registry — via moduleGrant or
# declaredModules — without re-reading live authority.
#
# THIS FILE ONLY EVER SHRINKS. A new entry fails
# TestEveryModuleCapabilityPathReReadsLiveAuthority; routing one means deleting
# its line.
#
# An earlier version of that gate watched only `moduleGrant`, so a function
# reading `declaredModules()` directly bypassed it and the gate was, in a
# reviewer's words, green about a NAME. Widening it to the registry read itself
# surfaced these paths. They are NOT all the same problem, and the file says
# which is which rather than implying one disposition:
#
# A. CAPABILITY DECISIONS that must be routed through
#    Service.AuthorizeModuleCapability. These are the real outstanding work.
#
# B. WRITES made under a capability already authorised upstream. They re-read the
#    registry to resolve a declared value rather than to decide authority, so
#    routing them would re-run a decision their caller already made — but they
#    are listed because "my caller checked" is exactly the assumption that rots
#    when a new caller appears.
solution_audit_events.go:admitDeclaredAuditEventTypesWritten
solution_audit_events.go:releasedAuditNamespace
source_delegation.go:recordSourceDelegationsTx
#
# C. NOT capability decisions at all: accessors and listings over the registry,
#    reached by paths with their own authorisation. They need a disposition other
#    than routing — most likely an explicit marker — and until that exists they
#    are here rather than silently excluded by name inside the gate, because
#    excluding them there would be the gate's author deciding what counts.
service.go:ModulePrincipals
layered_access.go:ListCollectionAccess
module_capabilities.go:ModuleContentResources
# HostAudiences resolves the host's AUDIENCE VOCABULARY — the closed set of
# strings this deployment serves a capability to (issue #952). A declared module
# prefix is one of its three members, which is why it reads the registry.
#
# It is group C's shape and not group A's, and the reason is sharper than
# "accessor": there is no authority decision here to route, because there is no
# CALLER in it. It answers "is this string one this host serves", a question with
# no tenant, no installation and no principal — asked BEFORE any authority is
# resolved, by requireVocabularyAudience, whose own caller then makes the
# authority decision with the live re-reads that belong to it
# (enforceActorCeiling, resolveAuthority). Routing it would need a caller it does
# not have.
#
# The registry half lists delivered prefixes as vocabulary; naming a module
# grants it no authority. Its capability paths check the fenced grant. The
# other half — the declared, non-tombstoned solution bindings
# — is read live from the database on every call, deliberately uncached, so a
# withdrawn solution leaves the vocabulary at once.
work_context_audience.go:HostAudiences
# ListPlatformCatalogue reads the registry to LIST the modules it knows, for a
# platform administrator's catalogue. It is group C's shape — an accessor, not a
# decision — and it is authorised upstream as a platform-admin RPC.
#
# It is on this list because of a change, not a regression: main read
# `s.modulePrincipals` as a bare field, which this gate does not watch, and the
# merge moved it to the `declaredModules()` accessor so the atomic pointer is
# loaded safely. The gate saw it for the first time as a result. That is the gate
# working — a direct field read was a way past it — and the honest disposition is
# to list the path rather than go back to the spelling that hid it.
platform_catalogue.go:ListPlatformCatalogue
